I have no idea what LSJ's specific reasoning is but, from my own
experience in other arenas[0], highly public "playtesting" tends to:

- result in a lot of heat and noise, but not much light. People shout
*a lot*. Note that some cards / mechanics / whatever will change
massively over time, and you can generate a lot of abuse and
frustration as each tweak and twist is used to psychoanalyse exactly
how stupid the designers are.

- lots of *bad* theory. Testing things out theoretically is useful and,
to an extent, necessary. However, this can quickly descend into
willy-waving of the "In *my* Assamite deck, this would pwn you in teh
FAEC, so shut up." "Thats only cos u've never sene mi Gionavvi
PUNCHnMUCNH u asshat." Repeat ad nauseum.

- a decline in actual testing. You'd be surprised just how much better
testing can be with a small group of 5 people on it, rather than a
sprawling group of 30. A couple of friends came to me one time and
begged me to do a code review of a revamped area they'd designed,
because the playtesters weren't doing it. Playtesters were walking up
and down going "Oh, how pretty" but not actually finding the things
they were supposed to - bugs, typos, suggestions for how to make it
better, sub-optimal commands. With so many more people "testing",
everyone could just assume that someone else would do it.

- false expectations. If I've designed a bunch of Aim cards and had to
scrap them because they just weren't right, for some reason, people
will whine.

- false expectations (2) - because I've just made the best suggestion
EVER to make Hag's Wrinkles better, LSJ will obviously include it in
the set exactly as written.

- hysteria and nuance. When sending things to large groups of players,
there will be inevitable loss of nuance. That paragraph you wrote
about how this is just a brainstorming session? Lost. You're trying
out a half-dozen different ideas, but only intend to print one, maybe
two? No, you're definitely creating six massively overpowered cards
for the Sabbat, and the Camarilla are just fucked because LSJ hates
the Camarilla and why are you still buying this game you fool?

- time. Sifting through feedback from a small group is more manageable
than having to go through bitchfests from a couple of hundred people.
Additionally, open playtests will inevitably mean that people bitch on
the newsgroup, the WW forums, various national forums, IRC, mailing
lists, a few quick-ish real-time JOL games... That's a lot of places
to try to manage, and LSJ obviously only has 24 hours available in a
day and a family to look after too!

- some decisions are taken because they're right, not popular. e.g.
grouping. Also, LSJ can potentially try out a set while leaking
possible card rewrites/bans to a small group of playtesters. "Yeah,
could you try out these new Inner Circle vamps? We're thinking of
toning down PTO or banning it, so don't worry overly about that."

- not wanting every single difference between the final texts and what
gets printed to be analyzed, with ensuing abuse being hurled at the
layout editor or printers. "What? You gave her ani instead of ANI?
You fucking suck. SACK HIM."

- facilities. Experience suggests that there are some issues with
getting the White Wolf website updated, which is likely to be a
problem for timely updates and changes.

Which isn't to say that the current system is necessarily optimal.

- In the past, the create-a-card poll was well received - though I feel
the actual options offered were a bit meh. (Also, long before that,
there was a "Who's your favourite vampire to be printed?" which I
think gave us Hesha.) A few more things like that wouldn't
necessarily be bad.

- Ideas have openly been sought for expansions (which I think gave us
Kindred Most Wanted, from Matt Green), and some "pre-design" decisions
were openly discussed (such as the composition of Final Nights).

- The WW LJ blog often gives a sort of "view from the bunker" about a
given product, and titbits about how things are going. They're
clearly not open playtests (which would be horrific), but they do
provide useful communication.

>Why are we to be "surprised" with new sets?

Marketing. Giving an "exclusive" preview to influential magazines or
websites. Managing expectations if things go awry. Excitement.
Pre-release buzz.

>How about posting cards and mechanics that are in playtesting for all
>players to make comments about?

Some cards and mechanics have been mentioned before, such as early
drafts of cards in White Wolf Quarterly, and similar. I remember Web of
Knives Recruit (I think) turning up in one.

>In this way we might prevent the unplayable/too powerful/stupid cards
>from ever being printed.

Won't happen. There are plenty of cards that have taken months and
years to exploit properly. There are also plenty of cards that are
taken as being the best thing since sliced bread, but in real, sober
play, they just don't work like that.

on said MUD, and a consumer of other games.

On Oct 1, 3:20 am, as...@hotmail.com wrote:

> The discussion about if or if not White Wolf playtest the new sets
> enough on various threads lead me to a question - why are the new sets
> so very secret? Why are we to be "surprised" with new sets?

Surprise is, I'm sure, something that some folks like about new sets.
But more than that, I suspect NDA/secret playtesting makes the process
work better for all involved. Having been involved in the playtesting
process in the past, I can say that I would prefer if playtesting were
slightly less secret than it has been (i.e. it would be nice if
separate playtest groups could compare notes). But as to doing it all
in the open, that strikes me as far more counter productive than not.

> How about
> posting cards and mechanics that are in playtesting for all players to
> make comments about? What do you think?

I suspect it would be incredibly chaotic. And filled with a lot of
noise and smoke, and not much actual playtesting.

> In this way we might prevent the unplayable/too powerful/stupid cards
> from ever being printed.

Probably not. Things like this happen. It is not possible for
playtesting to catch everything. Things like weak cards and too strong
cards slip throught the cracks, as there isn't really a way to prevent
it. When you are presented with a pile of playtest cards, you look for
ones that are interesting or possibly too powerful (as cards that are
too powerful are way worse than cards that are weak). And you tend to
focus on those--you build a deck to break card X, play it a few times,
send in a report, get the next playtest file, see what changed, keep
trying to break card X, send in a report, and so on. I can say with
certainty that in the past, I have helped turn cards that were wildly
over the top, power wise, into much more reasonable cards. Cards that
are weak tend to not get much attention, unless they are incredibly,
obviously weak (you should have seen the *original* version of
Tourtured Confessions...). 'Cause cards that are weak don't inspire
much attention, and unless they are measurably weak on paper, they
probably aren't going to see much play in playtest. So cards that look
generally average, but might be under the curve, tend to slip through.
As playtesting takes a long time and a lot of effort (you need to see
a card that looks like something that needs testing, figure out a way
to see if it is broken, build a deck, play that deck multiple times,
hope the card sees play in those multiple games, hope you aren't
ousted before the card becomes an issue, and so on), you do the best
you can, but accept that every once and a while, something will slip
through the cracks. As it always does.

-Peter

Here's a very rough synopsis of previous playtesting:

WW selects a subset of the playerbase comprised primarily of
individuals that have previously demonstrated an understanding of
rules/game balance/critical thinking and an interest in participating
in such talks - including people who consistently post well-thought-
out and coherent analysis to a variety of forums and the NG. They
don't select -every- player that meets this criteria, but select
enough of them to form a manageable sized pool. Not every person
approached is able to participate, but many of them do.

Those individuals then form playtesting groups out of their playgroups
as best serves their purpose, coordinating and summarizing their
findings into single reports (as opposed to each member of a group
submitting their own thoughts.) A lot of these groups include multiple
people out of that "experienced and analytical" subset.

Sets are then tested through multiple iterations, with each iteration
providing WW with a dozen or more lengthy, coherent responses and
analyses from the various groups.

Alternately, you can do open playtesting, where instead of the above,
you have hundreds and hundreds of replies, many of them fragmentary,
including a number of posts by players with limited experience, poor
understanding of the rules, and little to no concept of game balance
or critical thinking.

Personally, I'd rather not see a playtesting environment where the
design team has to read through comments made by players who just
picked up the game a month ago, or whose group plays with nothing but
variant rules (like the 4CL groups that still exist), or who just the
day before posting 'I think this card sucks ass' was asking 'so how
does intercept work?' and waste hours of time trying to go through
threads looking for the nuggets of useful feedback among the chaff.

And beyond a certain point, 'more playtesting' isn't helpful - there's
a point where the usefulness of having more people providing
commentary is offset by both redundancy and the time needed to process
the comments.

-John Flournoy

done open playtesting for a CCG, namely Shadowfist.

I playtested for the game in both of its phases, the owned-by-a-
company phase and a owned-by-a-group-of-players phase. The first was
not secretive, but you had to sign something. For the second, it
kinda became a free-for-all. PT was never entirely open, but the
majority of the player base participated and knew what was going on
and discussed it ad nauseum.

The major problems with open testing were twofold. One, tons of
light, very little heat in terms of comments. When we went to phase 2
the design team tried to set up a system for rating cards, and it
kinda worked, but it still seemed that subjective considerations
frequently trumped game design parameters. Lots of different
perspectives, but lots of assessments not based on either cohesiveness
of the set or how cards and strategies fit into the overall design of
the game.

Two, the amount of comments was staggering, and everyone wanted to be
heard and considered. I think part of the reason that the last set
for the game has taken sooo long to put together, and why some of the
design team resigned, was because of the playtest format. Too much
info, too many personalities, and too many tangents. It did not help
that playtest sets were enormous and all playtest groups got the
entire wad of cards.

I PTed for two sets, but just kinda lurked after that. I found that
my comments got buried in an avalanche of disagreements and verbose
comments not formatted to talk about game design. While I think the
current VTES playtest system could be improved, I don't think open PT
is the way to go.

Cheers,

John

A much more effective way to limit bad cards is to have professional
playtesters, a highly organized playtest process with a playtest
coordinator, clear direction, a good system of communication, and to
have plenty of time.

Might mean nothing to you, but I think it's an apt comparison. I was
brought in as were some other playtesters to help design a CCG
expansion. The company had a design file with ideas gathered from
various sources, mostly from public forums. Yes, people's posted card
ideas were actually noticed by someone. Our first task was to mine
that file of something like a 1000 card ideas. All together, we
thought maybe 50-80 ideas were worth looking at, not using, just
looking at as ideas for cards. Figure that's about the level of
signal to noise you will get from the public - less than 10% of what
is said by some random person in the player base is worth listening
to.

There are a lot of reasons for this. A major one is that lots and
lots of people who play CCGs don't think in the way that you want out
of designers and developers. Lots don't think in terms of the good of
the game but in terms of making something they like better or screwing
something they don't like. They don't think in terms of how something
fits into a greater whole. They don't analyze the numbers. They
don't analyze the metagame impact. They don't know the rules well
enough. They don't want to do the actual tedious work of
playtesting.

And, it is tedious. Once I started playtesting and then saw the
comments of people bitching and moaning about how awesome it must be
to be a playtester and how they would be awesome playtesters if only
given a chance, I started wishing everyone was forced to playtest at
least once to see just how annoying it is when done correctly. Sure,
there are some fun things about it, mostly what I remember is getting
to play hideously broken decks that led to cards getting fixed before
print or getting to play unlimited copies of ultrarares (before you
found out that they were going to be ultrarares and that the player
base was going to be shafted since you needed the cards to compete at
the highest levels). People have an overinflated view of their
importance/brilliance. There are plenty of opinions I form on reading
cards that don't prove to be true. There's plenty of playtesting I've
done that was insufficient. There are all sorts of cards I wish I had
spoken up about to make stronger but lacked the time. There's plenty
of rules questions I can't answer even for a game in which our group's
timing rules became the timing rules in the game because the game came
out without actual timing rules.

The facts of the matter are that niche CCGs don't have better testing
because of money, i.e. having professionals playtest, and that the
best CCG playtesting in the world - Magic's - still sees mistakes
made. That stuff is discovered later that wasn't caught by
playtesters is not only inevitable, but it's desirable from a
company's standpoint. CCGs are not supposed to be solvable. Their
attraction lies in the fact that there is an infinite amount of
discovery.

Yes, this part is particularly problematic.

Even with the (necessary) step of trying to identify people who are
going to be useful, there's no real way of communicating what testing
involves until they actually do it, for real.

My experience on a MUD was that players will also often overestimate:

1) their ability to test
2) the value of their testing.

The MUD kept fairly good reports of reports filed, reports
implemented/denied, and so on, so you could keep a fairly crude check on
what players were doing, and then follow it up with more in-depth
conversations (with players, coders etc. as necessary). In any number
of cases, the people co-ordinating the playtesters would check up on
people who didn't appear to be doing all that much. They'd wildly
overestimate the amount of bugs they'd filed, the amount of work they'd
done, the conversations they'd had with creators, and so on. They
possibly were doing lots of playing and having fun, but weren't doing
the testing.

The people *actually* doing the useful testing had to put in no end of
hard work, trying things out, filing reports, having discussions on a
given bug/suggestion, trying out the fixes, iterating over this, and so
on. And were, obviously, in a small minority of those who ever applied
to be playtesters.

They've sold that particular product. Thing is, orders for one set
(from distributors, that is) are based on the performance and purchase
history of past sets. So, if you're a distributor and the past two
sets sold out from your ordered stock and made you a bunch of money?
You'll order a good amount of the next set, even though you can't know
how it'll sell. If WW prints it fairly small, they'll then sell out.
If the past two sets were wildly unpopular, and your orders declined
and you've still got a bunch of product? You'll order small on the
next set, and WW is not likely to sell out.

So WW probably doesn't care, in the short term, whether player
reception of NoR has an impact - they've already sold it. But I'm
fairly certain they care in the long run, where folks order or don't
order future sets based on the reaction that NoR got.

(This, by the way, is one of the factors that effectively killed
Rolling Thunder as a release model: The first two or three mini-sets
to come in off the pipe all got advance-ordered by retailers and
distributors who knew nothing about them as if they'd sell just like
any other expansion up to that point, as opposed to at about one-third
the rate, since they were about one-third the size. When all that
over-ordered product sat on the shelves, or was horribly over-ordered
by customers in turn, the whole thing was proclaimed a dismal
failure.)

- D.J.

> companies," it is to hand it over to the public at large via the
> player base, under the premise that the players accessing the
> information is going to have a positive effect.

The original post asks why playtesting is secret. The desire to not
divulge proprietary information in a competitve market is a very
significant reason, and in my opinion is the most important one.
Playtest groups sign non-disclosure agreements that have legal
ramifications if they are violated, because the company considers
divulging that information to be potentially harmful and costly. If
there was no potential harm to the company, they wouldn't bother with
the lawyers.

> The side effect that other companies will have access to the information
> is assumed to not be problem.

One can't separate it from the equation.

> I don't know if this is true or not, but it is disingenuous to represent the
> argument as "handing out the information *to* the other companies, as
> opposed to handing it out to players.

There's no difference. By making playtesting public, the
information is made available to other companies.

> White Wolf could, for example, hand their developmental information to
> other companies and still not open playtests to the public.

Sure, but White Wolf (well, CCP now) can't hand their developmental
information to the public without handing it to other companies.

- Ben Peal

Well, it's a huge drag - and that's what's wrong with it. And the fact

actually DOES know what they're doing. Not everyone is Robyn Tatu's cat,
after all.

someone plays a permanent on the table, everyone in the game needs to

you're concerned about locations otherwise.

more useful. Find it too restrictive in use.

pressing combat decks or celerity decks, and you can at least cycle it
freely if not.

Community Justice - Far too high an opportunity cost. I could see
maybe one thrown in for flavour, but could easily be replaced with
more useful cards.

more work than the benefit. Most bleed decks would have better
options, but the fact you can add more bleed to it is a bonus.

underpowered. Negating maneuvers is most likely to be an unused
effect, presses a little more useful. Can be useful, I just can't see
putting it in a deck over other options.

So 3 cards out of what, 110? Perhaps I'm too lenient, but I found
Lords of the Night to be an extremely strong set with hardly anything
that could be considered wall paper or outright unplayable.

Well, ok. That is what the card is for. Providing bounce to decks that
have no bounce discipline. As bounce is strong. Because Lost in
Translation requires you to be an older vampire (and it costs 2
blood), it can't just willy-nilly get thrown into any bounceless mono-
discipline deck. Especially as bounceless mono-discipline decks tend
to run pretty small (i.e. all examples you give--mono-potence, mono-
animalism, and mono-celerity--generally are weenie decks). And decks
with small vampires tend to not be older than the bleeders. And tend
not to have a ton of blood for the 2 blood bounce.

Where Lost in Translation is strong is in decks that use big vampires
and don't come with bounce disciplines. Large Settites (Nakthortheb,
say). Eze vote decks. Big vampire superstar decks (Cock Robin and
Enkidu both have mutli acting and untapping capabilities, are large,
don't have bounce disciplines, and often act as superstars in
superstar decks). Yes. You have to make room for them. But even in a
blocky Cock Robin deck, having 3 or 4 Lost in Translations can be
*huge*--someone comes to bleed you for a bunch. You try and block with
your 2 or 3 Raven Spies. They manage to stealth past. You play Lost in
Translation, sending a 4 stealth bleed of 5 to your prey, which they
totally didn't see coming. This is where Lost in Translation is good.
And when it is good, it is very good. And that it exists at all means,
again, whenever you bleed someone, you can't just assume that they
can't bounce you, as long as they are older than you and have 2 blood.

Yes. It is true that big vampire superstar decks aren't that difficult
to build with stray dominate for bounce, as big vampires aren't that
hard to find with light dominate stuck on here and there. Or build a
deck with 5 superstars and 7 dominate weenies. But Lost in Translation
opens up even more areas for experimentation, and gives you the
opportunity to avoid the "Oh. This deck would be awesome. If only I
could get some bounce in..." part of deck building that hinders so
many deck plans. Is it better than, or even as good as, Deflection?
No. Of course not. And expecting it to be is just foolish. But it is a
good card that changes the game environment up significantly. And can
be very useful if the appropriate decks.

-Peter

I think it's your definition of 'wallpaper' that is raising the
arguments. Wallpaper usually refers to a card that is made pointless
due to another card doing much the same thing but cheaper (i.e.
Chainsaw is wallpapered by Gas-powered Chainsaw. Both have the exact
same effect, but Chainsaw is more expensive), or a card that has too
strict an opportunity window or too costly an effect (Eyes of the
Dead, Mummify, Mercy for the Weak, etc.).

To consider, for example, +1 bleed at +1 stealth at inferior as
wallpaper seems out of place. True, a Setite pre/obf deck would bleed
more effectively, perhaps, with more cards needed to do so. But a deck
focused on Serpentis, such as Entice decks, or Temptation/Corruption

"Are you on crack?" implies "That idea is totally insane. I can't even

Similarly, there are many other phrases that do not imply the literal
meaning of their words. Examples:

- "Are you out of your tree?" does not imply that you have a tree, that
you live in a tree, and that you have now left the tree. It implies
that the speaker thinks you're nuts.

- A journalist describing someone as "tired and emotional" does not, in
general, imply that they were either tired or emotional. It implies
that they were likely to be drunk and/or on drugs.

- "Man, that tasted like shit" does not, in fact, imply that your
cooking tastes like faeces. It just wasn't very pleasant.

- "Look what the cat dragged in" can be uttered by people where there is
no cat. It does not imply you have a cat. It does not imply you like
cats. It does not imply you have train your cat to drag things in.
It could be uttered in front of someone who is allergic to cats
without causing them to panic.

- A camp utterance of "Ooh, get her!" in response to a catty or bitchy
statement does not necessarily imply that the target of the statement
is female, or that they need to be 'got'.

- "He's sleeping with the fishes" does not imply some sort of
trout-related erotic need. Well, except in that one episode of The
Simpsons.

English is full of statements that are not meant to be taken literally.
"Are you on crack?" is one of them.
